## Design & invariants

The key schedule's code lives in the `tls13` module (`tls13.keyschedule.dtls13`, shared with
`tlsserver`); `src/keyschedule.zig` is a shim that binds it to the names below (only
`deriveSequenceNumberKey` is defined here), and the KATs live with it. `certverify` is
`tls13.certverify`, re-exported as `dtls.certverify` (`src/root.zig`; the signer burns
`ecdsa_burn`/`ed25519_burn`/`rsa_burn` are in `tls13/src/burn.zig`; `stackprobe_test.zig` still
measures `certverify.sign` from here). The (EC)DHE key exchange is `tls13.kex`; `Connection.zig`
keeps the group policy and wrappers named `ecdheGenerate`/`ecdheSharedSecret`/
`ecdheServerExchange`. `engine.Transcript` is `tls13.transcript.Transcript(Sha256)`.

The crypto-core layer (`keyschedule.zig`, `aead.zig`) is KAT-validated and the handshake flight
engine (`Connection.startHandshake` / `.handleFlight` / `.poll`) is a real RFC 9147 §5 PSK-only
and, additively, `.cert_dhe` certificate-authenticated client+server handshake, proven by an
in-memory client↔server interop suite (`Connection.zig`'s tests, `root.zig`'s module doc) and by
live wolfSSL runs in both roles (see *Live third-party interop*). HelloRetryRequest is
implemented in both roles and both key-exchange modes, including RFC 8446 §4.1.4's group change.
0-RTT and resumption are not implemented and not stubbed (see Backlog).

**Layered, like this repo's other DTLS/TLS-family scaffolds
(`opcua`/`noise`/`x509`):** the wire-framing layer (`record.zig`,
`handshake.zig`, `flight.zig`, `messages.zig`) is real, pure, allocation-free
where practical, and operates only on caller-supplied byte slices — no I/O,
no wall-clock calls (`flight.zig`'s timer takes `now_ms` from the caller),
no key material. The crypto-core layer (`keyschedule.zig`, `aead.zig`) holds the
key material. `Connection.zig` wires the two together: `Config.validate`,
`clientInit`/`serverInit`, the application-data record path
(`installApplicationKeys` + `send`/`recv`), and `startHandshake` /
`handleFlight` / `poll` (the flight engine).

**DTLS 1.3 does not reuse TLS 1.3's key-schedule labels unchanged:** RFC 9147 §5.9 changes the
HKDF-Expand-Label prefix to `"dtls13"` (no trailing space), so the key schedule uses its own
`expandLabel` parameterized on that prefix rather than `std.crypto.tls.hkdfExpandLabel`.

## RFC 9147 recon vs. `std.crypto`

Recorded in detail in `root.zig`'s module doc comment (single source of truth per
CONVENTIONS.md §5) — summary: a single-block AES-ECB primitive exists for the RFC 9147 §4.2.3
sequence-number mask (`std.crypto.core.aes.Aes128/Aes256.initEnc(key).encrypt(...)`). std's
AES-CCM exports only 13-byte-nonce presets and its generic `AesCcm` is not `pub`, while the
TLS/DTLS 1.3 profile needs a 12-byte nonce, so the CCM suites run on the sibling `aesccm` module. Nothing else in
`std.crypto.tls` is reusable: transcript hashing and HelloRetryRequest/cookie handling are inline
in `tls.Client.init`'s private state machine, not separate types.

## Key schedule and record-protection primitives

All in `src/keyschedule.zig` (names bound to `tls13.keyschedule.dtls13`) unless noted. Each
function's doc comment names its RFC section; all fifteen are implemented and KAT-validated:

1. `keyschedule.earlySecret` — RFC 8446 §7.1, `HKDF-Extract(salt=0, IKM=PSK)`.
2. `keyschedule.binderKey` — RFC 8446 §7.1, `Derive-Secret(early_secret,
   "ext binder", "")`.
3. `keyschedule.pskBinder` — RFC 8446 §4.2.11.2, the PSK binder itself
   (HMAC over the truncated ClientHello1 transcript with a
   `"finished"`-labeled key derived from `binder_key`). **Most
   security-critical item in this module** — a wrong/skipped check lets an
   attacker splice a PSK identity across connections.
4. `keyschedule.deriveHandshakeSecret` — RFC 8446 §7.1, handles both
   `psk_ke` (zero IKM) and `psk_dhe_ke` (real (EC)DHE shared secret) modes.
5. `keyschedule.deriveHandshakeTrafficSecrets` — RFC 8446 §7.1, `"c hs
   traffic"`/`"s hs traffic"` labels.
6. `keyschedule.deriveMasterSecret` — RFC 8446 §7.1.
7. `keyschedule.deriveApplicationTrafficSecrets` — RFC 8446 §7.1, `"c ap
   traffic"`/`"s ap traffic"` labels, transcript through server Finished.
8. `keyschedule.deriveFinishedKey` — RFC 8446 §7.1, `"finished"` label.
9. `keyschedule.computeFinishedVerifyData` — RFC 8446 §4.4.4, `HMAC
   (finished_key, transcript_hash)`; verifier side MUST compare in constant
   time (`std.crypto.timing_safe.eql`), never `std.mem.eql`.
10. `keyschedule.deriveTrafficKeyIv` — RFC 8446 §7.3, `"key"`/`"iv"` labels
    (the AEAD key + RFC 9147 §4.2.1's static IV).
11. `keyschedule.deriveSequenceNumberKey` — RFC 9147 §4.2.3, `"sn"` label
    (DTLS-specific, no TLS 1.3 equivalent).
12. `aead.Protection(Aead).nonce` — RFC 9147 §4.2.1, `static_iv XOR
    (epoch, sequence_number)` bit-packing — confirm exact byte placement
    against the RFC text.
13. `aead.Protection(Aead).protect` / `.unprotect` — RFC 9147 §4.2, AEAD
    seal/open of the DTLSInnerPlaintext (RFC 8446 §5.2 shape, reused
    unchanged) with the unified header as additional data.
14. `aead.encryptSequenceNumberAes` / `decryptSequenceNumberAes` — RFC 9147
    §4.2.3, AES-ECB-derived keystream mask over the on-wire sequence-number
    bytes.
15. `aead.encryptSequenceNumberChaCha20` / `decryptSequenceNumberChaCha20`
    — RFC 9147 §4.2.3's ChaCha20-suite equivalent (confirm it is NOT simply
    the AES path with the cipher swapped before assuming so).

## Certificate mode (RFC 8446 §4.4, additive to the PSK core)

`Connection.zig` implements certificate-mode Certificate/CertificateVerify/CertificateRequest
(`messages.zig` framing + `certverify.zig` sign/verify + `certauth.zig`'s DER/std-Certificate
bridge), layered on top of the unchanged PSK key exchange — see `root.zig`'s module doc
"Certificate mode" section and `Connection.zig`'s own "certificate mode" section (right before
`handleFlightServer`) for the design rationale.

- **Implemented:** Certificate/CertificateVerify/CertificateRequest wire
  framing; server always presents its cert when `Config.cert` is set;
  optional mutual auth via `Config.request_client_cert` +
  `Config.require_peer_cert`; peer-chain trust via `Config.peer_verify`
  (`.none` / `.trust_anchor` — a real one-hop `std.crypto.Certificate
  .Parsed.verify` check via `certauth.verifyLeafAgainstAnchor` — /
  `.chain` — RFC 5280 §6 path validation through the `x509` module,
  `certauth.verifyPeerChain` — / `.verify_fn` escape hatch); real ECDSA-P256/P384, RSA-PSS, Ed25519
  signatures over the LIVE running transcript (not a fixed KAT string) via
  `certverify.sign`/`.verify`, unmodified. Proven by a real client↔server
  self-interop suite in `Connection.zig` (server-cert-only, mutual auth,
  wrong-key rejection, untrusted-anchor rejection, required-but-absent-cert
  rejection) — same in-memory-oracle style as the PSK suite, no external
  peer.
- **`signature_algorithms` extension negotiation (RFC 8446 §4.2.3):** the ClientHello (both `.psk`
  and `.cert_dhe` modes) and a server's `CertificateRequest` now advertise
  `Config.signature_algorithms` (defaults to every scheme `certverify.zig`
  implements) for real; `Connection.zig`'s `selectSignatureScheme` picks the
  scheme a CertificateVerify signs with from the intersection of the peer's
  advertised list, `Config.signature_algorithms`, and
  `certverify.candidateSchemes(cc.private_key)` (what the configured key's
  FAMILY can actually sign under — RSA keys offer all three
  `rsa_pss_rsae_sha*` schemes, EC/Ed25519 keys exactly one each), failing
  with `error.NoSignatureSchemeOverlap` rather than a silent default when
  there is no overlap. `verifyPeerCert` additionally rejects (`error
  .SignatureSchemeNotAdvertised`) a peer's CertificateVerify that used a
  scheme THIS side never put in its own `signature_algorithms` — a downgrade
  guard, checked before the signature itself. `CertConfig` carries no
  fixed `signature_scheme` field.
- **RSA base-blinding cache:** `CertConfig.rsa_blinding` (an `rsa.BlindingCache`, OpenSSL's per-key
  `BN_BLINDING`, as `tlsserver`'s `CertifiedKey.rsa_blinding`) is handed to every RSA signature this side
  makes — the 1.3 CertificateVerify (`certverify.signWith`), the 1.2 CertificateVerify and ServerKeyExchange,
  PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5 (`sig12.sign`). Null (default) draws a fresh blinding per signature. Not thread-safe:
  one cache per thread. Test: `conn12_test.zig` "CertConfig.rsa_blinding".

- **Untrusted DER.** `std.crypto.Certificate.parse` (Zig 0.16; the reader is unchanged in 0.17.0)
  is not panic-safe against malformed or adversarial DER — fuzzing crashed it with trivial
  few-byte or random inputs via an unguarded array index in std's ASN.1 walker — and Zig has no
  exception mechanism to intercept that. Both `certauth.zig` entry points (`parseLeafPublicKey`,
  `verifyLeafAgainstAnchor`) therefore route PEER-supplied Certificate bytes through this
  collection's `x509` module's bounds-checked `spkiOf`/`safeCertificate` bridge first and never call
  `std.crypto.Certificate.parse` directly — the same hardened parser `iec62351` and `opcua` use.
  See `certauth.zig`'s module doc ("CLOSED GAP" note) and its test `parseLeafPublicKey:
  adversarial DER returns a typed error instead of panicking` (empty/truncated/malformed DER and a
  full truncation sweep of a real certificate, all typed-error, no crash). `.cert_dhe` mode
  parses peer certificates through the same path.

## Cert-only (EC)DHE mode (RFC 8446 §4.2.8 key_share + X25519)

The genuine (EC)DHE-based, PSK-less certificate-only key exchange is a distinct handshake
mode, selected by `Config.key_exchange = .cert_dhe` (default `.psk`, so every PSK /
cert-over-PSK path and its RFC 8448 KATs are unaffected). Summary:

- **`messages.zig`:** `key_share` (RFC 8446 §4.2.8, ClientHello list +
  ServerHello single-entry forms), `supported_groups` (§4.2.7),
  `signature_algorithms` (§4.2.3) encode/decode, plus the `NamedGroup` enum.
  **X25519** (`0x001d`), **secp256r1** (`0x0017`) and the PQ hybrid
  **X25519MLKEM768** (`0x11ec`, see the threat-model
  section) are wired end to end; a fresh ClientHello offers a share in
  `Config.key_share_group` (default X25519) and any other advertised group
  is used when a server names it in a HelloRetryRequest (RFC 8446 §4.1.4).
  `key_share`
  has a THIRD wire form for that message — a bare two-byte `selected_group`
  (`encode`/`decodeKeyShareHelloRetryRequest`), not interchangeable with the
  ServerHello form.
- **`Connection.zig`:** in `.cert_dhe` mode the ClientHello offers
  `{supported_groups, signature_algorithms, key_share}` with a fresh
  ephemeral X25519 keypair (`std.crypto.dh.X25519`, seeded from the
  caller-supplied `Entropy`) and **no `pre_shared_key`, no binder**; the
  ServerHello returns its own X25519 share. The ECDHE shared secret is fed
  into the **existing, unmodified** `keyschedule.deriveHandshakeSecret` (the
  early secret's IKM is the zero PSK, RFC 8446 §7.1 — the schedule was
  already DHE-capable, this only supplies the secret; the function was NOT
  forked). Server-only auth and mutual auth (`request_client_cert`) both work,
  reusing the same `certverify`/`certauth`/cert-message plumbing as
  cert-over-PSK mode. The ephemeral private key **and** the shared secret are
  `std.crypto.secureZero`-wiped as soon as the handshake secret is derived
  (forward-secrecy hygiene), and again in `deinit`.

**Validation / honesty:**
- **External-vector KAT (RFC 8448 §3):** the X25519 key_share computation
  (`recoverPublicKey` + `scalarmult`, both directions) and its feed into the
  key schedule reproduce RFC 8448 §3's published client/server X25519
  private+public keys, the `8bd4054f…` shared secret, and the derived
  early+handshake secrets byte-for-byte. §3 is a psk_dhe_ke trace, but its
  ECDHE math is identical and its early secret is over an all-zero PSK —
  exactly this mode's construction.
- **Live third-party peer (no external BYTE vector):** the full cert-only
  wire FLOW (ClientHello→ServerHello→{EE,[CertReq],Cert,CertVerify,
  Finished}→…). **No public DTLS 1.3 cert-only byte-trace exists**, so there
  is no KAT for the flow itself; instead it is driven end to end against a
  live wolfSSL 5.9.1 certificate server (PSK-less X25519 (EC)DHE + an ECDSA
  P-256 chain that must verify against this repo's own trust anchor), and
  additionally at a 256-byte peer MTU so the Certificate arrives fragmented.
  The in-memory client↔server suite remains for the paths a single live peer
  cannot drive — mutual auth and the reject-teeth (tampered ServerHello
  key_share, wrong CertificateVerify key, untrusted anchor, missing
  key_share). Going live immediately found a defect of exactly the class
  self-interop cannot find: the `.cert_dhe` ClientHello carried no
  `supported_versions`, so a real server negotiated DTLS 1.2.

  Certificate authentication is also driven live in both directions: a wolfSSL
  server with `VERIFY_PEER | FAIL_IF_NO_PEER_CERT` and the fixture anchor as its
  only CA verifies OUR client's Certificate + CertificateVerify (mutual auth), and a
  real wolfSSL certificate CLIENT verifies the chain our server presents
  (`wolfSSL_get_verify_result` asserted inside the peer). The mutual-auth run found
  a defect of the same family as those listed under *What it found*: the client decoded a CertificateRequest's
  `signature_algorithms` into a fixed `[8]u16`, so a real peer's list
  (wolfSSL sends 16) came back `TooManyExtensions` → `Malformed` — the same
  mistake the ClientHello path had already been fixed for, surviving here
  because only our own server had ever sent a CertificateRequest.

- **secp256r1 ECDH KAT (Python `cryptography` / OpenSSL 3.5.5):** two fixed
  scalars, their SEC1 uncompressed points, and the ECDH output — which for
  the NIST curves is the shared point's X COORDINATE only (RFC 8446 §7.4.2),
  not the point encoding. An independent oracle, since the RFC 8448 vector
  covers only the X25519 half.


## Post-handshake: KeyUpdate, exporter, ALPN

API:

- **KeyUpdate** (RFC 9147 §8, RFC 8446 §4.6.3/§7.2).
  `Connection.requestKeyUpdate(request_peer)` queues one;
  `Config.key_update_after_records` (default 2^24, the RFC 8446 §5.5 AES-GCM
  margin; `null` = off) queues one automatically from `send`. `poll(now_ms,
  out)`, once connected, returns the control
  records this side owes, one record per call: the ACK for processed
  post-handshake messages, then the queued KeyUpdate, then — timer-gated —
  a retransmission of an un-ACKed KeyUpdate in a fresh record. The write key
  switches only when an ACK names a record that carried the KeyUpdate
  (§8: "MUST NOT send records with the new keys ... until the previous
  KeyUpdate has been acknowledged"). `recv` on a peer KeyUpdate returns the
  new `error.ReceivedKeyUpdate`: the read key moved to the next secret, the
  previous one is kept (one generation, §8 "MUST retain the pre-update
  keying material"; §4.2.2 epoch reconstruction picks it by the 2 epoch
  bits), an ACK is queued and, for `update_requested`, so is this side's own
  update unless one is pending or the 2^48-1 epoch ceiling forbids it (§8
  overrides TLS's "MUST respond"). A retransmitted KeyUpdate only re-ACKs. A
  NewSessionTicket is ACKed and ignored (no resumption). Request values
  other than 0/1, a wrong length, a KeyUpdate under the previous epoch, or
  any other post-handshake type is `error.Malformed`. New errors:
  `ReceivedKeyUpdate`, `KeyUpdatePending`. Epochs are `u64`
  (`write_epoch`/`read_epoch`).
- **Exporter** (RFC 8446 §7.5). `Connection.exportKeyingMaterial(label,
  context, out)` over `exporter_master_secret` (derived with the
  application secrets via `tls13.keyschedule.deriveApplicationSecrets`),
  with RFC 9147 §5.9's `"dtls13"` HKDF-Expand-Label prefix — so the bytes
  differ from a TLS 1.3 exporter over the same secret. Bounds are errors
  (`LabelTooLong`, `OutputTooLong`); `NotConnected` before the handshake.
  This is what DTLS-SRTP keying (RFC 5764's `"EXTRACTOR-dtls_srtp"`) needs.
- **use_srtp** (RFC 5764 §4.1). `Config.srtp_profiles` (preference order, at most
  `max_srtp_profiles` = 16, no 0x0000 — `error.InvalidSrtpProfiles`). Client: offers the list with an empty MKI
  (1.3 ClientHello; 1.2 ClientHello). Server: its first preference the client also listed — OpenSSL's server picks
  from its own list the same way — answered with an empty MKI (§4.1.1 option 2: "return an empty srtp_mki value to
  indicate that it cannot make use of the MKI") in EncryptedExtensions (1.3, RFC 8446 §4.2's table: CH, EE) or the
  ServerHello (1.2); no overlap means no answer (§4.1.1), not an error. Client: the answer must be one profile it
  offered and carry no MKI (§4.1.3 aborts on an MKI other than the one offered), else `error.Malformed`. Result:
  `negotiatedSrtpProfile()` on `Connection`, `Connection12` and `Endpoint`; the SRTP keys are
  `exportKeyingMaterial("EXTRACTOR-dtls_srtp", null, out)` (§4.2). Self-interop in both engines; not yet driven
  against a live peer.
- **ALPN** (RFC 7301). `Config.alpn_protocols` (preference order, each name
  1..255 bytes, encoded list ≤ 256 bytes — `error.InvalidAlpnProtocols`).
  Client: offered in both ClientHello forms; a server answer must be one
  name it offered (`error.Malformed` otherwise). Server: its first
  preference the client also offered goes into EncryptedExtensions; an offer
  with no overlap is `error.NoApplicationProtocol` (§3.2). Result:
  `Connection.negotiatedAlpn()`. The client's EncryptedExtensions buffer grew
  64 → 512 bytes, so a server's other EE extensions still fit.

**Validation:** no published DTLS 1.3 KeyUpdate or exporter vector exists
(RFC 8448 has neither); the tests are the RFC 9147 §8 Figure 14 exchange in
both suites, the next read key re-derived independently from RFC 8446 §7.2's
`"traffic upd"` label, late previous-epoch records, a lost KeyUpdate and a
lost ACK, the exporter equal on both sides and distinct from the TLS-prefix
exporter. **Against a live peer (wolfSSL 5.9.1, PSK mode):** four interop cases. `psk-client-alpn`: our ClientHello offers
`h3`, `coap`; wolfSSL (accepts only `coap`) answers in EncryptedExtensions, `negotiatedAlpn()` is `coap` and the peer prints
the same. `psk-server-alpn`: wolfSSL offers `h3,coap`, our server (preference `coap`, `h3`) picks `coap`, and the peer exits 0 only
if the answer it parsed is `coap`. `psk-client-keyupdate-ours`: we send a KeyUpdate with `update_requested`; wolfSSL ACKs it and answers with its own,
both epochs go 3 -> 4, and a message and its echo cross under the new keys. `psk-client-keyupdate-theirs`: wolfSSL calls
`wolfSSL_update_keys` and writes under the new key; `recv` reports `ReceivedKeyUpdate`, our `poll` answers with the ACK and, because wolfSSL
asked for it, our own update (two control records), the epochs go 3 -> 4 and the data decrypts. The transcript replays all of it,
including the control records `poll` emits (new ops `request_key_update`, `poll`, `poll_idle`, `expect_epochs`; `expect ... alpn=`).
Both KeyUpdate cases have wolfSSL as the SERVER; the engine is role-symmetric here, but a wolfSSL KeyUpdate in the client role is not recorded.
The first `poll` after an update request also carries the ACK of wolfSSL's NewSessionTicket (two records, not one).

**An ACK in the middle of a handshake flight.** RFC 9147 §7.1 has a receiver ACK a partial flight (out-of-order or late records; SHOULD), and the ACK travels in the highest epoch the sender holds (§7: equal or higher than the acknowledged records), so a peer may place one in epoch 0 (plaintext content type 26, §4) or epoch 2 among the records of its flight. The two handshake record readers now accept it: the body is length-checked like a post-handshake ACK (`error.Malformed` for a short, truncated, odd-sized or over-long list), an epoch-2 ACK runs the same AEAD and replay-window checks as any record, and the record is then skipped. It is never added to the ACK this side owes (§7.1: ACKs only for handshake records), and an epoch-2 one marks the records of our flight it names (below). **Fully ACKed flights:** §7.2's "Once all the messages in a flight have been acknowledged, the implementation MUST cancel all retransmissions of that flight" is met. the cached flight keeps, for each record, the handshake fragment it carried and its (epoch, sequence_number) (`beginFlight` / `recordPiece` / `cacheFlight`), an epoch-2 ACK marks the ones it names (`noteFlightAck`; an exact (epoch, sequence_number) match, so a number we did not send, in any epoch, is ignored), and the timer is cancelled once all are marked. The marks survive `handleFlight`'s rollback (an ACK-only datagram is an incomplete flight, and a rollback would otherwise undo the cancel); only an authenticated record can set them. An epoch-0 ACK stays length-checked and skipped: it is unauthenticated, and an off-path sender naming our predictable epoch-0 numbers would otherwise silence our ClientHello. Ignoring an ACK only costs a conforming retransmission. **Partial retransmission (§7.2 SHOULD):** a retransmission (`poll`'s timer) re-seals only the pieces no ACK named, each in a NEW record with a fresh epoch-0 / epoch-2 sequence number — RFC 9147 §5.2: "From the perspective of the DTLS record layer, the retransmission is a new record. This record will have a new DTLSPlaintext.sequence_number value" (the 1.2 engine already did so, as wolfSSL does in both versions). An ACK that leaves part of the flight unacknowledged makes `handleFlight` re-send the rest at once (§7.2: "SHOULD retransmit the unacknowledged messages or fragments"), returned in `out` with `need_more_data`. Only the latest record number of each piece is kept, so a late ACK naming an earlier transmission of it costs one more retransmission. **Partial-flight ACKs (§7.1 SHOULD):** a server whose `handleFlight` is left with part of the client's final flight answers with an epoch-2 ACK naming the records read so far (up to `max_ack_records`, 16). A client cannot: it commits the ServerHello, and with it the handshake keys an ACK is sealed under, only with its complete flight 2 (an incomplete parse is rolled back), and flight 2 is implicitly acknowledged anyway. Reference behaviour: the live interop runs against wolfSSL lose no datagram, so no partial-flight ACK from it was observed (its source is not read).

**Send-side fragmentation (RFC 9147 §5.5).** With `Config.max_datagram_len` set, every handshake message whose record would exceed it — epoch-0 hellos (a hybrid ClientHello is ~1.4 KB) and sealed epoch-2 messages (worst-case 22 bytes of record overhead: 5-byte unified header, content type, 16-byte tag) — is sent as consecutive fragments of the same `message_seq`, one record each; `record.nextDatagram` packs the records into datagrams. Without a limit a message larger than one 1500-byte record is split the same way (before, it failed with `BufferTooShort`). The transcript hashes the unfragmented message (§5.2), so peers see no difference. A cached flight holds at most `max_flight_records` (64) records and `max_flight_bytes` of fragments; a mutual-auth hybrid cert flight at the 128-byte minimum fits.

## Cipher suites and the suite hash

Wired: `aes_128_gcm_sha256` (0x1301), `aes_256_gcm_sha384` (0x1302),
`chacha20_poly1305_sha256` (0x1303), `aes_128_ccm_sha256` (0x1304) and
`aes_128_ccm_8_sha256` (0x1305, RFC 7925's constrained-device suite) — the CCM pair on the
`aesccm` module's 12-byte-nonce `Aes128Ccm` / `Aes128Ccm8`, with the AES sequence-number mask
(RFC 9147 §4.2.3: CCM is AES-based). Under CCM_8 a record whose ciphertext would be shorter
than the 16 bytes the mask samples is zero-padded (DTLSInnerPlaintext padding; §4.2.3 "Senders
MUST pad short plaintexts out"), and the receiver strips it as for any padding. CCM is opt-in
(not in the default list). Default `Config.cipher_suites` is
`{ aes_128_gcm_sha256, aes_256_gcm_sha384 }` — pion/dtls's and wolfSSL's
order, the mandatory suite first. API:

- `CipherSuite.hash() HashAlg` (`.sha256` / `.sha384`). Every secret,
  transcript hash, PSK binder and Finished MAC is `Hash.length` bytes for
  the negotiated suite (RFC 8446 §7.1). They live in 48-byte buffers sliced
  to the suite's length; `suitehash.zig` holds the runtime `inline else`
  wrappers over the comptime-typed `tls13.keyschedule`, so the schedule
  itself is the one `tls13` tests for both hashes.
- The transcript (`suitehash.Transcript`) runs SHA-256 and SHA-384 side by
  side until the suite is known — a client offering both learns it only
  from the ServerHello or a HelloRetryRequest — then drops the other.
  `Hash(ClientHello1)` for RFC 8446 §4.4.1's `message_hash` is read from it
  under the retry suite's hash.
- `Config.psk_hash` (default `.sha256`). RFC 8446 §4.2.11: "each PSK is
  associated with a single Hash algorithm"; in `.psk` mode the binder uses
  it, a client offers only suites of that hash (so the default PSK
  ClientHello is unchanged), a server selects only those
  (`error.NoCipherSuiteOverlap` otherwise), and a client refuses a
  ServerHello (`error.NoCipherSuiteOverlap`) or HelloRetryRequest
  (`error.IllegalHelloRetryRequest`) naming another.
  `ConfigError.PskHashMismatch` when no configured suite has the PSK's hash.
  A binder of the other hash's length is `error.Malformed` at the server.
- HelloRetryRequest cookie: `version || suite || Hash(ClientHello1) ||
  HMAC-SHA256`, the hash at the suite's length (67 or 83 bytes); the MAC
  stays HMAC-SHA256 (this server's own integrity check, not protocol).
- `Connection.installApplicationSecrets(suite, client, server)` takes
  slices of the suite's hash length; `installApplicationKeys` keeps its
  `*const [32]u8` signature and refuses a SHA-384 suite.
- KeyUpdate and the exporter run under the suite's hash (exporter cap 255 ×
  48 bytes for SHA-384).

**Validation:** no published DTLS 1.3 SHA-384 trace exists (RFC 8448 is
SHA-256 only). The SHA-384 schedule is pinned by `tls13`'s SHA-384 KATs and
`suitehash`'s wrapper-vs-comptime tests; the wiring by self-interop in PSK
(`psk_hash = .sha384`, a 48-byte binder on the wire), cert-DHE, a client
offering both hashes against a server preferring either, PSK and cert-DHE
HelloRetryRequest (83-byte cookie, stateless second connection), KeyUpdate
(Figure 14, and the next read key/IV/sn key re-derived with HKDF-SHA384
from the 48-byte secret), the exporter (equal to an independent HKDF-SHA384
export, 255 × 48 cap), and the PSK-hash refusals above. Live: the PSK
handshake under `TLS13-AES256-GCM-SHA384` with a 48-byte SHA-384 PSK runs against wolfSSL 5.9.1
in both roles, with and without a HelloRetryRequest cookie (`tools/interop.zig` cases
`psk-client-aes256`, `psk-client-aes256-hrr`, `psk-server-aes256`, `psk-server-cookie-aes256`);
ChaCha20-Poly1305 and certificate mode under SHA-384 are not driven against a live peer.

## DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) and version negotiation

Owner decision. API (a `Config` that does not set `versions` runs the 1.3
engine, unchanged):

- **`Connection12`** — the 1.2 engine, with `Connection`'s method shape
  (`clientInit`/`serverInit` from the same `Config`, `startHandshake`,
  `handleFlight` → `HandshakeResult`, `poll`, `send`, `recv`,
  `exportKeyingMaterial`, `negotiatedAlpn`, `deinit`; plus
  `negotiatedSuite`). Requires `.dtls12` in `Config.versions`.
- **`Endpoint`** — `union { v13: Connection, v12: Connection12 }` with the
  same methods, picking by `Config.versions`. With both versions the 1.3
  engine starts; its ClientHello then also carries 1.2 in
  `supported_versions`, the 1.2 suites, `extended_master_secret`, an empty
  `renegotiation_info` and `ec_point_formats`. A client that sees a
  HelloVerifyRequest or a ServerHello without `supported_versions`, or a
  server that sees a ClientHello not offering 1.3, gets the internal
  `error.NegotiatedDtls12` from the (rolled-back) 1.3 engine, and
  `Endpoint` hands the exchange to `Connection12`, which continues from the
  very same ClientHello (splicing a HelloVerifyRequest cookie into it if
  asked). RFC 8446 §4.1.3's downgrade sentinel: a 1.2 server whose config
  allows 1.3 ends `ServerHello.random` with `DOWNGRD\x01`; a 1.2 client
  whose config allows 1.3 refuses it (`error.DowngradeDetected`).
- **Config:** `versions` (default `{.dtls13}`), `cipher_suites12` (default
  pion's order: ECDHE_ECDSA AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305,
  the same three for ECDHE_RSA, PSK AES-128-GCM, ECDHE_PSK
  ChaCha20-Poly1305; a connection uses only the ones `key_exchange` allows —
  PSK suites in `.psk`, the certificate suites otherwise),
  `require_extended_master_secret` (default true), `psk_identity_hint`,
  `max_datagram_len` (see "Fragmentation").
  `hello_retry` doubles as the HelloVerifyRequest cookie key + peer
  binding; `cert`/`peer_verify`/`expected_peer_name`/`request_client_cert`/
  `require_peer_cert`/`signature_algorithms`/`alpn_protocols` mean what they
  mean in 1.3.

**Wire behaviour.** Full handshakes only (RFC 5246 §7.3 with RFC 6347
§4.2's 12-byte headers, which the transcript hashes too, §4.2.6). Record
protection RFC 6347 §4.1.2.1 over RFC 5288 (GCM: 4-byte salt + 8-byte
explicit nonce = this record's epoch‖sequence) and RFC 7905 (ChaCha: IV xor
epoch‖sequence). Key derivation `prf12.zig` (RFC 5246 §5 P_SHA256 /
P_SHA384, RFC 7627 master secret, key block, Finished, RFC 5705 exporter).
ECDHE groups X25519, secp256r1, secp384r1 (`tls13.kex`). Signatures
(`sig12.zig`): every `tls13.certverify` scheme except ML-DSA, then
`rsa_pkcs1_sha256` / `rsa_pkcs1_sha384` (1.2 only — RFC 8446 §4.2.3
forbids them in 1.3), our preference order, so RSA-PSS wins whenever the
peer offers it. HelloVerifyRequest: DTLS 1.0 version, the ClientHello's
record sequence number, HMAC-SHA256 cookie over the peer binding and RFC
6347 §4.2.1's client parameters; the server keeps nothing (the whole
`handleFlight` is rolled back), and a stateless server accepts a
ClientHello at any `message_seq`. A client answers at most three
HelloVerifyRequests. `renegotiation_info`: a client sends it and requires it
in the ServerHello; a server answers the extension or the SCSV, refuses a
non-empty one, and also serves a client that signals
neither, without sending the extension (RFC 5746 §4.3 lets a server that
never renegotiates continue; OpenSSL, wolfSSL and mbedTLS servers do, and
Debian's wolfSSL 1.2 client, built without `HAVE_SECURE_RENEGOTIATION`, is
such a client — found by the live interop, our server refused it with
`SecureRenegotiationRequired`). A client keeps requiring it, as OpenSSL 3's
does by default. A HelloRequest or a new ClientHello after the handshake is
ignored (`ReceivedPostHandshakeMessage`).
Retransmission: the last flight is cached as messages and re-encoded with
fresh record numbers (timer in `poll`, or a duplicate of the peer's
previous flight); a connected server answers a client's retransmitted final
flight through `recv` (`ReceivedPostHandshakeMessage`) + `poll`. Every
`handleFlight` is a transaction (rolled back on error). A peer alert is
`error.ReceivedAlert` (`peer_alert` holds it); this module sends none.

**Fragmentation (RFC 6347 §4.2.2/§4.2.3).** *Send:*
`Config.max_datagram_len` (default 0 = off, the earlier behaviour) is the
largest datagram this side emits. An epoch-0 handshake message whose record
would exceed it is split by `handshake.Fragmenter` (the 1.3 engine's), one
fragment per record, each record within the limit; a retransmission
re-fragments the same way under fresh record numbers. The bytes a
`handleFlight` / `poll` returns are then several datagrams, cut by the pure
`record.nextDatagram(bytes, max_len)` (greedy, whole records, a record over
the limit alone, never split; it reads DTLSPlaintext/Ciphertext and unified
headers, so it serves 1.3 output too). Epoch-1 handshake (Finished, 24 bytes)
always fits: `Config.validate` refuses a limit under
`min_max_datagram_len` = 128 (`error.MaxDatagramLenTooSmall`; OpenSSL refuses
link MTUs under 256, wolfSSL and pion set no floor). Default 0 because the
caller must split: pion defaults to an MTU of 1200, wolfSSL and OpenSSL take
the socket's (about 1400 / 1472 on Ethernet), mbedTLS to 0 like here. The 1.3
engine does not fragment on send yet and ignores the field (Backlog).
*Receive:* the message in progress is reassembled by `handshake.Reassembler`
(as in 1.3): fragments in any order, duplicates absorbed, a contradicting
overlap refused (`OverlappingFragment` / `InconsistentLength` /
`InconsistentMessageType`, where the earlier code said `Malformed`).
Fragments of a LATER message are queued — RFC 6347 §4.2.2 says SHOULD when
there is buffer space, wolfSSL and OpenSSL do (pion buffers a whole flight)
— up to 8 messages ahead and 6144 bytes in all (the largest flight this
engine accepts fits in reverse order), and fed in when their turn comes;
beyond that they are dropped and retransmitted. A stateless server at
`.start` queues nothing. The queue is unauthenticated, so a call that fails
after feeding a queued fragment — or while the message in progress holds
queued bytes from an earlier call — is retried once from its own datagram
with the queue (and that message) emptied: a forged later-message fragment
cannot wedge the genuine flight (tested with 4000 forged fragments, among
them a complete forged message, and with one latched by an earlier call). The epoch-0 replay window records a record only once it advanced
the handshake (see "Epoch-0 replay window"), so queued forgeries do not shadow the genuine records either.


**Epoch-0 replay window.** An epoch-0 record proves nothing, so it may not move the replay window
on its own say-so. Rule followed: RFC 6347 §4.1.2.6 ("the receive window is updated only if the MAC
verification succeeds") and RFC 9147 §4.5.1 ("The window MUST NOT be updated due to a received record
until that record has been deprotected successfully"). The mandatory RFC rule decides; the model is
pion/dtls (`replayMarker` returns a no-op marker for epoch 0 until the version is chosen, and
`bufferHandshakeRecord` marks a packet valid only after `fragmentBuffer.Push` accepted the fragment) and
wolfSSL's DTLS 1.3 path (`Dtls13UpdateWindowRecordRecvd` only once stateful); OpenSSL and wolfSSL's
DTLS 1.2 path record every epoch-0 record, which the mandatory RFC rule does not allow. In the 1.2 engine an
epoch-0 record is checked against the window first and recorded only after it completed a message (the
next expected `message_seq` moved on) or was an accepted ChangeCipherSpec (the read epoch moved on)
(`Connection12.processRecord`, `Progress`), and even then only if it moves the high mark at most one window
width (64) past the current one, or past 0 before any (`Window.recordUnauthenticated`,
`src/Connection12.zig`); a record further ahead is processed but not recorded. A duplicate, a partial
fragment, a queued later message, an early ChangeCipherSpec, epoch-0 application data or a stateless
HelloVerifyRequest exchange leave the window untouched. Companion rules: `handleFlight`'s retry-once from live
bytes also drops a message in progress from an earlier call (not only the queue), but keeps the retry's
result only if the datagram alone COMPLETES the message — otherwise the partial message and the error
stand, so a forged fragment cannot evict a genuine partial one; and a server at `.start` lets a WHOLE
ClientHello under another `message_seq` replace a partial one (a mere fragment does not). The 1.3 engine
keeps no epoch-0 receive window at all (`hs0` counts sends only; duplicates are recognised by
`message_seq`), so it is not affected. The residual risks are in *Threat model*.

**Plain-PSK premaster.** The plain-PSK premaster buffer is `2 + max(80, max_psk_len) + 2 + max_psk_len`
bytes (`Connection12.zig`, `:1080`), because RFC 4279 §2's `other_secret` is `psk.len` zero bytes; the cap
`max_psk_len` is 512 (OpenSSL's `PSK_MAX_PSK_LEN`). The DTLS 1.3 PSK path has no such buffer (the PSK goes straight
into HKDF-Extract; an over-long PSK identity is a typed `BufferTooShort` from the ClientHello's
pre_shared_key buffer).

AES-128-CCM and CCM_8 for 1.2 (RFC 6655 §4 PSK, RFC 7251 §2 ECDHE_ECDSA: `psk_with_aes_128_ccm`
0xC0A4, `psk_with_aes_128_ccm_8` 0xC0A8, `ecdhe_ecdsa_with_aes_128_ccm` 0xC0AC,
`ecdhe_ecdsa_with_aes_128_ccm_8` 0xC0AE — RFC 7925 §4.2 / §4.4 mandates the two CCM_8 ones) run
on `aesccm` with RFC 6655 §3's salt ‖ 8-byte explicit nonce (the GCM layout) and tags of 16 / 8
(`record12.Bulk.aes_128_ccm` / `.aes_128_ccm_8`, checked byte for byte against `aesccm` in
`record12.zig`); opt-in, not in `default_suites`, so a default ClientHello is unchanged.

`use_srtp` (RFC 5764) is negotiated in the hellos, as in 1.3 (*Post-handshake* section).

**Connection ID (RFC 9146).** `Config.connection_id` works in the 1.2 engine too: the `connection_id` extension (54)
in the ClientHello, answered in the ServerHello by a server that set one (a client CID over `max_cid_len` is declined,
as in 1.3); once negotiated, every epoch-1 record this side sends — the Finished included — is a `tls12_cid` (25)
record carrying the peer's CID when the peer asked for a non-empty one (`record12.sealCid`): `DTLSInnerPlaintext` =
content ‖ real type, no padding, and the RFC 9146 §5.3 additional data (`seq_num_placeholder` of eight `0xff`,
`tls12_cid`, `cid_length`, `tls12_cid`, version, epoch, sequence number, CID, inner length), pinned byte for byte in
`record12.zig`. A received epoch-1 record must be a `tls12_cid` record with this side's own CID when that is
non-empty (another CID, or none, is `error.Malformed`, RFC 9146 §3), and a `tls12_cid` record on a connection that
expects none is `error.Malformed`. `Connection12.peerConnectionId()` / `Endpoint.peerConnectionId()`;
`record.nextDatagramCid` cuts `tls12_cid` records. Self-interop (all three AEAD families, an empty client CID,
fragmented certificate flights); no live peer: Debian's wolfSSL 5.9.1 negotiates it, then its client fails `connect`
with -320 (build message failure) and its server goes silent at our CID-protected Finished.

Deliberately not implemented in 1.2: see *What is deliberately not done*.

## Threat model / out of scope

- **Not provided — see Backlog (not silently skipped):** session resumption /
  `NewSessionTicket` (no `"res binder"`/resumption-PSK path — only `"ext
  binder"`/externally-configured PSK), 0-RTT/early data.
- **Connection ID (DTLS 1.3, RFC 9146 §3 / RFC 9147 §9).** `Config.connection_id` (≤ `max_cid_len` = 32, mbedTLS's
  default cap; `error.InvalidConnectionId`): a client offers it in the ClientHello, a server that set one answers in
  the ServerHello (a peer CID longer than 32 bytes: the server does not negotiate, a client fails `Malformed`). Once
  both sent it, every protected record from epoch 2 on carries the peer's CID (unified header C bit; Figure 15 of RFC
  9147 puts it on EncryptedExtensions already), and a received record must carry this side's own CID — another one,
  or none while a non-empty one is expected (RFC 9146 §3 "MUST be treated as invalid"), is `error.Malformed`. An
  empty own CID means the peer sends none. `Connection.peerConnectionId()`; the sender's records are cut into
  datagrams with `record.nextDatagramCid`. A caller that demultiplexes by CID reads it at byte 1 of the record.
  **CID updates (§9):** `offerConnectionIds(cids, .immediate | .spare)` sends a NewConnectionId (up to
  `max_new_cids` CIDs, each the length of this side's negotiated CID, which is how received records are parsed),
  `requestConnectionIds(n)` a RequestConnectionId; one such message at a time, retransmitted by `poll` until an ACK
  names one of its records (`connectionIdUpdatePending`). Received records may then carry the old CID or any newly
  issued one. A received NewConnectionId with `.immediate` switches the CID this side sends at once and keeps the
  rest as spares (`peerSpareConnectionIds`, switch with `usePeerConnectionId`; at most `max_cid_spares`, oldest
  dropped); a received RequestConnectionId is reported by `connectionIdsRequested` until answered with `.spare`.
  Both are ACKed and surface as `ReceivedPostHandshakeMessage`; on a connection without a CID, or malformed, they are
  `error.Malformed` (RFC 9147 §9: unexpected_message). The CID updates are self-interop only. Self-interop (with fragmentation at 128 bytes) and live against wolfSSL 5.9.1 in both roles
  (`psk-client-cid`, `psk-server-cid`, live-only: not in the committed transcript).

- **Post-quantum key exchange.** `X25519MLKEM768`
  (0x11ec, draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem) is wired end to end in both roles:
  the 1216-byte client share (`ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key ‖ X25519 public`
  — ML-KEM FIRST, the draft's famous naming inconsistency), the 1120-byte
  server share (`ciphertext ‖ X25519 public`), and the 64-byte
  `ss_MLKEM ‖ ss_X25519` concatenation into the SAME key schedule the two
  classical groups feed. Server side is unconditional; client side offers
  the hybrid when `Config.key_share_group = .x25519_ml_kem768` (default
  stays `.x25519`, matching the field's opt-in tier — wolfSSL/mbedTLS —
  because a hybrid offer costs a HelloRetryRequest round trip against every
  classical-only DTLS server; the always-advertised `supported_groups` entry
  still lets a preference-honoring server retry a classical offer UP to it).
  Live-proven against wolfSSL 5.9.1 in three shapes: offered directly,
  reached via HRR upgrade, and a wolfSSL client's share answered by our
  server's encapsulation path.
  - **Server-side groups beyond the offer (2026-11-21):** a server also takes a client's share in
    secp384r1, secp521r1, ML-KEM-512/768/1024 and the SecP256r1MLKEM768 / SecP384r1MLKEM1024 hybrids
    (`accepted_groups`, after `advertised_groups` in preference), all computed by `tls13.kex` as for
    `tlsserver`; wolfSSL's DTLS 1.3 serves the same set. A client still offers only `advertised_groups`. The
    ServerHello bound grew to 1792 bytes for the largest server share (1665). Self-interop per group.
  - ⚠ The combiner trap `ssh` documents turned out to have a SECOND instance,
    in std itself: `std.crypto.kem.hybrid.MlKem768X25519` has exactly these
    share sizes but is **X-Wing** — a SHA3-256 combiner over
    `secrets ‖ ciphertext ‖ key ‖ label` — while TLS wants the bare
    concatenation, and `ssh` hashes `SHA256(ss_M ‖ ss_X)`. Three
    constructions, identical wire sizes, zero interop between them; this
    module transcribes the draft's own construction over
    the `mlkem` module's ML-KEM-768 directly.
  - Two wolfSSL field lessons, encoded in the interop harness: a PQ share is
    only generated after `wolfSSL_UseKeyShare` (`set_groups` alone yields an
    EMPTY client_shares list), and the `WOLFSSL_DTLS_CH_FRAG` build (auto-on
    when ML-KEM + DTLS 1.3 are both enabled) empties the key share whenever
    ClientHello1 would exceed the MTU rather than fragment it — both look
    like "peer didn't offer the group" from the other side.
- The PSK binder (`keyschedule.pskBinder`, `src/keyschedule.zig`) MUST be
  checked (server side) before trusting the offered PSK identity — a
  missing check is the single highest-impact bug this module could ship
  with. It is: the server recomputes it over the truncated ClientHello and
  compares in constant time (`timing_safe.eql`), failing with
  `error.BinderVerifyFailed` (`Connection.zig`).
- `aead.Protection.unprotect` must return the typed
  `error.DecryptionFailed` on any tag mismatch, never panic, never leak
  timing differences between "bad tag" and "bad padding"/other failure
  modes — attacker-controlled ciphertext must never reach a panic path.
- **Certificate paths and entries:** `.trust_anchor` stays a minimal one-hop check. `PeerVerify.chain`
  (`ChainVerify`: trust anchors, optional `required_eku`, optional CRL `revocation`) runs `x509.verifyChain` over
  every certificate of the peer's Certificate message (leaf + at most 8 intermediates, `certauth.max_chain_certs`):
  path building (out-of-order and cross-signed chains), validity at `Config.now_sec`, `basicConstraints` /
  `keyUsage` on each CA, path length and name constraints, `Config.expected_peer_name` against the leaf's SAN —
  Go `crypto/x509` / OpenSSL semantics, as the `x509` module documents. x509's working memory is a 32 KiB stack
  buffer (`FixedBufferAllocator`), so the module stays allocation-free; running out fails the chain. Both engines;
  checked when the Certificate arrives, before CertificateVerify. Anchored by a three-level chain from OpenSSL
  (`tools/gen-chain-certs.sh`, `openssl verify` OK): verified to the root, the intermediate as anchor; refused with
  the intermediate missing, a wrong name, a wrong EKU, a wrong root. The received Certificate message is still bounded
  by `max_cert_message_body` (1200 bytes). `CertificateEntry` extensions (OCSP stapling/SCT) are framed empty on send
  and length-validated-but-discarded on receive (Backlog).
- **The cookie exchange is not stateless against a FRAGMENTED ClientHello.**
  `serverProcessClientHello` fully reassembles the ClientHello (`takeHandshakeMessage`) before the cookie
  check ever runs — the cookie lives inside the ClientHello body, so it cannot be read from a partial one.
  A 26-byte datagram declaring a 2048-byte message with a 1-byte fragment returns `need_more_data` before the
  cookie logic (or `sendHelloRetryRequest`) is reached, and the caller cannot tell that apart from a
  legitimately fragmenting client — both produce an empty `out`. Each such source address costs the server one
  live `Connection` (~13 KB) held until `max_flight_bytes` forces `FlightTooLarge`: a ~500x memory
  amplification against a 26-byte packet, on the path §5.1's cookie exists to keep stateless.
  `sendHelloRetryRequest`'s "stores nothing" claim is true once reached — the gap is everything upstream of
  it. A real design tension: a legitimate peer with a large (e.g. PQ-hybrid) ClientHello genuinely needs to
  fragment, and `max_flight_bytes` bounds one connection's growth, not how many a caller ends up holding.
  **Opt-in refusal:** `HelloRetryConfig.refuse_fragmented_client_hello = true` refuses a ClientHello whose first
  record does not carry the whole message (`error.FragmentedClientHello`, before any reassembly), which closes the
  gap at the price of every client whose hello exceeds the path MTU. Reference behaviour: OpenSSL's `DTLSv1_listen`
  never reassembles a ClientHello (it reads the cookie from the first fragment only, `SSL_R_FRAGMENTED_CLIENT_HELLO`
  otherwise), mbedTLS's cookie check does not understand a fragmented one (Mbed-TLS issue #7549), and wolfSSL
  accepts a fragmented first DTLS 1.3 ClientHello only with cookies disabled (wolfSSL PR #11475). It is off by
  default because DTLS 1.3 differs from the 1.2 listen path those describe: a HelloRetryRequest cookie commits to
  `Hash(ClientHello1)` (RFC 8446 §4.4.1), so it cannot be minted from a first fragment, and here ClientHello2 also
  lands on a fresh stateless `Connection`, so the switch refuses fragmented hellos in both rounds — including a PQ
  hybrid ClientHello (~1.4 KB) on a 1280-byte path.
- **Cookie rotation.** RFC 9147 §5.1 RECOMMENDS accepting the previous `cookie_secret` for a period.
  `HelloRetryConfig` takes one secret; a caller wanting the overlap retries ClientHello2 under a second
  `Connection` configured with the older secret — caller policy.
- **DTLS 1.3 flight accumulation.** `max_flight_bytes` (`Connection.zig`) caps what is buffered
  unauthenticated; exactly one message is reassembled at a time. A peer that RETRANSMITS a whole flight it
  already sent, verbatim, into the middle of an incomplete accumulation is rejected (`handleFlight`'s "KNOWN
  LIMIT", `Connection.zig`) and the caller restarts; redundant fragments of the message being reassembled
  and retransmitted copies of consumed messages are absorbed. What it SENDS is split at `Config.max_datagram_len`
  (*Post-handshake* section, "Send-side fragmentation").
- **Epoch-0 residuals (1.2),** inherent to unauthenticated epoch 0; all are first-in-wins races an off-path
  sender could already run, and none is closed: (1) a forged partial latched AHEAD of, or a forged fragment with
  the right type/length/`message_seq` and wrong bytes arriving AFTER the first fragment of, a genuine message that
  the peer FRAGMENTS across datagrams blocks it by content (every later genuine fragment of that range is
  `OverlappingFragment`, and no single genuine datagram completes the message for the retry) until the caller's
  handshake timeout; the hellos travel whole unless `max_datagram_len` forces otherwise (the length is
  brute-forceable within `max_message_len`); (2) a forged WHOLE message under the expected `message_seq` replaces a
  genuine partial one through the retry; handlers of authenticated content (Certificate chain, ServerKeyExchange
  signature, Finished) still refuse it and the partial is restored, an unauthenticated one (ServerHello,
  ServerHelloDone, HelloVerifyRequest) is taken and the handshake then fails at Finished — no worse than the same
  forgery arriving first, and the retry processes such a message at most twice; in cookie mode a forged whole
  ClientHello only earns a stateless HelloVerifyRequest and changes nothing; (3) a forged HelloVerifyRequest that
  precedes the genuine one moves the client to `message_seq` 1, after which the genuine HelloVerifyRequest
  (`message_seq` 0) is an old duplicate and the client keeps resending its ClientHello with the forged cookie
  (bounded by `hvr_count`). Closing these would need authentication that epoch 0 does not have.
- **Replay of unrecorded epoch-0 records.** A record that is not recorded in the window is processed again when
  replayed verbatim: a replayed duplicate makes this side resend its flight once per replayed datagram, to the same
  peer address, with no growth (a forged duplicate under a fresh record number always could); queued later
  fragments are likewise re-queued, bounded by `max_future_bytes`. A forged record that does complete a message
  is message injection, which epoch 0 cannot prevent anyway (the Finished check fails it).

## What is deliberately not done

- **DTLS 1.2: CBC suites** (Lucky13 family), **static-RSA key exchange** (no forward secrecy, Bleichenbacher),
  **compression**, **renegotiation** (a HelloRequest or a new ClientHello after the handshake is ignored,
  `ReceivedPostHandshakeMessage`) and **DTLS 1.0** — each a security or scope choice, not an omission.
- **A server-side cookie expiry.** RFC 9147 §5.1 offers timestamps as an ALTERNATIVE to secret rotation, and
  rotation is what the API exposes; a clock would also be the first one this module reads.
- **A SERVER-initiated group change** (RFC 8446 §4.1.4). The client half is implemented (a retry naming another
  advertised group is answered with a fresh share in it, live-anchored against wolfSSL); this server takes
  whichever offered share it can use and answers a ClientHello with nothing usable with `error.MissingKeyShare`,
  never a group-change retry — deciding a group before the cookie verifies would mean holding more state for an
  unverified peer, which is what `sendHelloRetryRequest` exists not to do.
- **`psk_dhe_ke`.** `.psk` mode stays PSK-only, so a retry carrying a `key_share` there is
  `error.HelloRetryRequestUnsupported` (`Connection.zig`) rather than a silent upgrade to an exchange this
  engine does not run.
- **More than ONE in-progress inbound handshake message in the 1.3 engine.** A fragment of a later message
  arriving while an earlier one is incomplete is `error.InterleavedFragments` (`Connection.zig`) rather than
  buffered — the deliberate cap on attacker-driven memory (see `max_flight_bytes`); no conforming sender produces
  that ordering. (The 1.2 engine queues later messages, bounded.)

## Live third-party interop

`tools/interop.zig` runs real DTLS 1.3 handshakes over a loopback UDP socket
against **wolfSSL 5.9.1**, in both roles and in both PSK and certificate mode,
each followed by an application-data round trip — twenty-six cases in all (including ALPN in both roles and in
certificate mode, a KeyUpdate from each side in PSK and in certificate mode and a wolfSSL client's KeyUpdate against
our server, and the four AES-256-GCM-SHA384 PSK cases). The committed transcript holds twenty-two of them (Backlog:
re-capture).

**It is a PROGRAM, not a test, and that is the design.** A
zig-libs module is standalone Zig with no external dependency; an anchor against
a foreign implementation needs a C compiler and a system library, which a test
binary must not want (where that toolchain is missing a test would skip silently,
in CI, where the peer install is `continue-on-error`). The split:

- `tools/interop.zig` + `tools/wolfssl_peer.c` — outside the module, run by
  `zig build interop-dtls`, compiled (never run) by `zig build check-interop`.
  This is the only thing that can discover a NEW divergence, and it is a
  pre-release check.
- `src/testdata/wolfssl_transcript.txt` — what `--capture` records: every
  datagram in both directions, plus the seed, configuration and post-handshake
  assertions each case ran with.
- `src/wolfssl_replay.zig` — replays that transcript in pure Zig, with no
  wolfSSL, no C compiler, no child process and no socket, so the anchor's value
  runs in the per-commit lane.

**What pins the replay.** Our side draws every random byte from the
caller-supplied `Entropy` (std 0.16 removed `std.crypto.random`, so the module
has no hidden generator), and the live runs have always used its
`.seeded_for_test` arm from a fixed seed — originally so a failing interop run
could be re-run byte-for-byte. Nothing was added, weakened or stubbed to make
the replay deterministic; the transcript records the seed and the replay reads
it back.

**What the replay cannot do**, stated because a green run is weaker than it
looks: it cannot discover a new divergence (the peer's bytes are frozen at one
release); a failure is not proof of non-interoperability (a change that emits
different-but-still-valid bytes fails it without any peer having refused
anything — re-run the live program, and re-capture if it is green); and it
cannot re-check what was never on the wire — the peer's exit status, its
`wolfSSL_get_verify_result` and the `PEERCERT` subject it printed were checked
when the recording was taken and are kept in the file as comments.

The peer is a C program (`tools/wolfssl_peer.c`), read from its own
path and compiled with `cc -lwolfssl` when `zig build interop-dtls` runs. It is
not embedded in anything and it is not part of the shipped module; the program
fails with an actionable message (`sudo apt install libwolfssl-dev`) rather than
skipping, because unlike a test it is allowed to require its peer. wolfSSL has
`WOLFSSL_DTLS13`; OpenSSL has no DTLS 1.3 and GnuTLS stops at DTLS 1.2, so wolfSSL is the
only installable DTLS 1.3 peer.

**DTLS 1.2.** `tools/interop.zig` + `tools/wolfssl_peer.c` (modes `12-server-*` / `12-client-*`,
`wolfDTLSv1_2_*_method`) run fifteen cases against wolfSSL 5.9.1, recorded in
`src/testdata/wolfssl12_transcript.txt` (`zig build interop-dtls -- --capture --version 12`, a file of its
own so the 1.3 recording and the corpus counts derived from it stay put) and replayed by
`src/wolfssl12_replay.zig`: ECDHE_PSK ChaCha20-Poly1305 both roles (our identity hint and wolfSSL's) and
behind OUR stateless HelloVerifyRequest; ECDHE_ECDSA with AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM-SHA384 and
ChaCha20-Poly1305, on X25519 and secp256r1; ECDHE_RSA both roles; mutual authentication both ways (wolfSSL
verifies our 1.2 CertificateVerify, we verify its); wolfSSL's own HelloVerifyRequest on every client case;
wolfSSL fragmenting at a 256-byte MTU; our side fragmenting at 200 bytes in both roles. The live run found one
wire defect, fixed: the server's RFC 5746 requirement (above). Plain PSK (`psk_with_aes_128_gcm_sha256`), which
Debian's wolfSSL lacks (built without `WOLFSSL_STATIC_PSK`), runs against **OpenSSL 3.5** in both roles, in the same
capture and file: our client against `openssl s_server -dtls1_2 -listen` (its stateless HelloVerifyRequest) and an
`openssl s_client` offering only `PSK-AES128-GCM-SHA256` against our server (the identity hint in ServerKeyExchange);
the application data is checked on OpenSSL's stdout and back, seventeen 1.2 cases in all.

### What it found

Four wire defects, none of which self-interop could ever have caught — a
self-interop suite has both sides make the same mistake in lockstep:

1. **The ClientHello had no `legacy_cookie` field at all** (RFC 9147 §5.3).
   DTLS 1.3 moved the cookie into a HelloRetryRequest extension but keeps
   the legacy field, present and empty. Omitting it shifts every following
   byte, so the peer read the compression-methods length as half of
   `cipher_suites`' — `alert(fatal, decode_error)`.
2. **The PSK binder covered two bytes too many.** RFC 8446 §4.2.11.2 hashes
   the ClientHello "up to and including the `identities` field", i.e. with
   the whole binders **list** removed — and a list, being a vector, starts
   at its own 2-byte length prefix. Both sides here truncated 1 byte later,
   agreed with each other, and disagreed with everyone else:
   `alert(illegal_parameter)`, "binder does not verify".
3. **Neither Hello carried `supported_versions`.** Every version field on
   the wire reads DTLS 1.2 by design (RFC 9147 §5.3), so this extension is
   the only place the negotiated version appears. Without it a peer cannot
   tell 1.3 was meant. The client now sends it and *requires* it in the
   ServerHello (`error.VersionNotNegotiated` / `error.UnsupportedVersion`) —
   a downgrade guard, not just a compatibility fix.
4. **The server never ACKed the client's final flight** (RFC 9147 §7.1).
   The spec's list of implicitly-acknowledged flights is "handshake flights
   *other than* the client's final flight of the main handshake"; all others
   "MUST be ACKed". Nothing follows that flight to carry an implicit ack, so
   a silent server leaves a conforming client blocked in `connect` forever.

A fifth was a robustness bug rather than a wire bug: the server decoded a
peer's `signature_algorithms` into a fixed `[8]u16` and returned
`error.Malformed` when it overflowed. wolfSSL advertises 18 schemes and
OpenSSL a similar number, so any real client was rejected as malformed. The
list is now filtered against the schemes this module can actually select,
which bounds the buffer by OUR list instead of the peer's.

A **sixth** was the identical bug on the OTHER side of the same extension:
the CLIENT decoded a `CertificateRequest`'s `signature_algorithms` with
`decodeU16ListExtension` into a fixed `[8]u16`, so a real peer's list
(wolfSSL 5.9.1 sends 16) became `TooManyExtensions` → `Malformed` and mutual
auth against a third party could not complete at all. Only our own server
had ever sent a `CertificateRequest`, and its list is short — so the fix
applied to the ClientHello path never reached this one. Found the day the
live mutual-auth test was written; same `filterU16ListExtension` fix.

### Proven against wolfSSL: the HelloRetryRequest cookie exchange, both roles

RFC 9147 §5.1's return-routability check runs in both directions against a
real peer: our client against a default-configured wolfSSL server
(`server-hrr` peer mode), and our server — with `Config.hello_retry` set —
against a stock wolfSSL client. Both live tests assert the retry ACTUALLY
happened (`Connection.sawHelloRetryRequest`), so neither can silently decay
into a duplicate of the no-retry test if the exchange stops taking effect.

## Verification

- **Run:** `scripts/modtest dtls` (includes the hermetic wolfSSL replays of both transcripts; needs nothing
  external). `zig build check-interop` compiles the live interop program without running it; `zig build
  interop-dtls` runs the live wolfSSL cases (needs `libwolfssl-dev` and `cc`; `-- --version 12` for DTLS 1.2;
  `-- --capture` re-records `src/testdata/wolfssl_transcript.txt`, with `--version 12` the 1.2 file).
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run
  and the delta runs after it. Its killing tests are `src/audit_test.zig` (black-box: exact-size output buffers and
  one-past-the-limit lengths for every `messages` / `messages12` encoder, decoder edges, record / record12 /
  Reassembler / FlightTracker / AEAD / PRF boundaries, and for the 1.2 engine a fake peer that feeds crafted
  handshake records) and test blocks at the end of `Connection12.zig` and `Connection.zig` for the private helpers.
- **Anchors:** see *Anchoring*. The key schedule against RFC 8448 §3/§4 byte for byte and an independent Python
  `hmac`/`hashlib` reimplementation; the AEAD record protection against OpenSSL; the X25519 key_share and its feed
  into the schedule against RFC 8448 §3; secp256r1 ECDH against a Python-`cryptography`/OpenSSL KAT (the shared
  point's X coordinate only, RFC 8446 §7.4.2); the 1.2 PRF against Python `hmac`/`hashlib` goldens and std's own
  TLS 1.2 PRF, the 1.2 record nonces / AAD against std's AEADs (`record12.zig`); the live wolfSSL transcripts of
  both versions replayed byte for byte (`src/wolfssl_replay.zig`, `src/wolfssl12_replay.zig`). No published DTLS 1.3
  KeyUpdate, exporter, SHA-384 or cert-only byte trace exists, so those paths rest on self-interop, independent
  re-derivation in the tests and the live peer.
- **Self-interop (in memory):** every wired 1.3 suite reaches `.connected` with byte-identical keys, a real
  `send`/`recv` round trip, caller-clocked retransmission on a dropped ClientHello, and typed-error rejection of a
  wrong PSK, mismatched identity, corrupted ServerHello and a malformed HelloRetryRequest; certificate mode
  (server-cert-only, mutual auth, wrong key, untrusted anchor, required-but-absent certificate); `.cert_dhe` with
  its reject teeth (tampered ServerHello key_share, wrong CertificateVerify key, missing key_share);
  HelloRetryRequest in both modes and both hashes; KeyUpdate (RFC 9147 §8 Figure 14) and the exporter. DTLS 1.2
  (`conn12_test.zig`): all eight suites, PKCS#1 v1.5 against a client offering no PSS, mutual auth, untrusted /
  wrong-name certificates, wrong PSK / identity, HelloVerifyRequest (stateless, cookie refused for another peer
  binding), loss of flights, tampering with rollback, hand-built hellos for the EMS / RI / unoffered-extension /
  sentinel refusals, `Endpoint` in every version pairing; fragmentation at a 200-byte limit with the server flight
  delivered reversed and duplicated, a fragmented retransmission, the forged-fragment flood, `record.nextDatagram`
  at its boundaries; the epoch-0 replay window tests in `Connection12.zig` and `conn12_test.zig`; `Connection.zig`'s
  test that an injected epoch-0 record with a huge number does not affect the 1.3 engine.
- **Bench:** `zig build bench-dtls` (`tools/bench.zig`, ReleaseFast, no foreign side): the per-record AEAD call
  against a cached AES-GCM context, seal and open at 64..1400 bytes, gated on identical output, and the whole
  `send` + `recv` of a connected pair; prints the ratio and the spread of the rounds.
- **Fuzz:** `DTLS_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]` (testkit's deterministic driver; `_ONLY` selects a harness):
  `dtls-handshake` (PSK, HelloRetryRequest cookie and (EC)DHE with one flight damaged; certificate-authenticated
  flights are not driven), `dtls-record`, `dtls-wire`, `dtls-keyupdate` (`src/fuzz_test.zig`); `dtls12-handshake`
  (PSK, ECDHE_PSK, PSK behind a HelloVerifyRequest, ECDHE_ECDSA; one datagram damaged / random / dropped /
  duplicated; flights fragmented at `max_datagram_len` 128..600 in half the cases and in every reorder case,
  delivered datagram by datagram, and two datagrams of one flight swapped — undamaged, duplicated, fragmented or
  not the pair must connect, a reordered pair need not but must not panic and must agree on keys when it connects;
  reach pins `fragmented_connected` and `reordered_connected`) and `dtls12-wire` (the `messages12` decoders)
  (`src/fuzz12_test.zig`). The Smith (`--fuzz`) path of `dtls12-handshake` feeds the first datagram only.
- **Constant time:** `src/ctgrind_harness.zig` through `scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh dtls`: targets `hs`, `app` and `ku`
  (1.3: PSK through full handshakes under both hashes, record keys through send/recv, KeyUpdate both ways +
  exporter with traffic and exporter secrets tainted) and `hs12`, `app12` (1.2: PSK and ECDHE_PSK handshakes, the
  server's ECDHE key through an ECDHE_ECDSA AES-256-GCM-SHA384 one, record keys tainted); the expected rows are in
  `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`. The reported sites are the Finished / AEAD tag verdicts and the parsing of
  decrypted content, none a branch on a key.
- **Dead stack:** `src/stackprobe_test.zig`, `src/stackprobe2_test.zig` drive the burned entry points through full
  in-memory handshakes (PSK, cert X25519, cert P-256 with mutual auth, cert X25519MLKEM768; GCM, ChaCha20 and CCM;
  a server flight-2 retransmission through `poll`), and the HelloRetryRequest cookie flow (PSK and cert X25519: the
  first server's stateless retry, ClientHello2, a second fresh server; the cookie secret and its HMAC state are
  needles). The ECDSA nonce of each CertificateVerify a live handshake sent is a needle too: the probe opens the
  sender's epoch-2 records with its handshake keys, rebuilds the transcript, checks the signature and solves `k`
  from it. By design and not dead stack: the standalone helpers `keyschedule.*`, `aead.Protection`, `record.*`
  return secrets by value into the CALLER's frame, and the live `Connection` keeps `pending_ap_*`, `hs_*` keys and
  traffic secrets until `deinit`.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** a committed transcript of live interop vs a real wolfSSL 5.9.1 peer (both roles, both key exchanges, twenty-two flows), replayed byte-for-byte by `src/wolfssl_replay.zig` with no wolfSSL present, and a second one of seventeen DTLS 1.2 flows (fifteen against `wolfDTLSv1_2_*_method`, two plain-PSK ones against OpenSSL 3.5, `src/wolfssl12_replay.zig`); the live exchanges themselves are `tools/interop.zig` (`zig build interop-dtls`)

## Backlog / deferred

- **AEAD record protection is the stateless per-record call** of the `aesgcm` module: every record re-runs the
  AES key expansion and the GHASH key setup. `zig build bench-dtls` (`tools/bench.zig`) measures it against a cached
  `aesgcm` `Context` (first run, 2026-11-21, ReleaseFast, 3 rounds on a loaded machine, spread up to 40 %): cached /
  per-record 0.20–0.23 at 64-byte records, 0.31–0.35 at 256, 0.52–0.58 at 1024, 0.61–0.65 at 1400 (AES-128 and
  AES-256, seal and open); a whole `send` + `recv` of 64 bytes on AES-128-GCM is ~1.2 µs, of which ~0.6 µs is the two
  per-record AEAD calls. The rewrite (per-epoch `Context` storage behind `Protection(Aead)`, which ChaCha20 shares
  without needing it) waits for a quiet-machine A/B with the spread below the effect.
- **Re-capture of the 1.3 transcript.** Four live 1.3 cases (`psk-server-keyupdate-theirs`, `cert-client-alpn`,
  `cert-client-keyupdate-ours`, `cert-client-keyupdate-theirs`) pass against wolfSSL 5.9.1 but are not yet in
  `src/testdata/wolfssl_transcript.txt`: `zig build interop-dtls -- --capture --version 13`, then
  `wolfssl_replay.zig`'s `recorded_cases_floor` 22 → 26 and `fuzz_corpus.zig`'s pinned frame counts.
- **Session tickets / resumption and 0-RTT**, for both engines. Saves a handshake on constrained links; pion has it for
  1.2, wolfSSL for 1.3. Effort: medium (sibling `tlsresume` covers the server ticket seal for TLS). Fits §2.
- **`CertificateEntry` extensions** (OCSP stapling `status_request`, SCT): wolfSSL and OpenSSL offer stapling.
  Framed empty on send, length-validated-but-discarded on receive. Needs an OCSP response verifier (the `x509`
  module checks CRLs). Effort: medium.
- **A second independent stack.** wolfSSL agreeing with us rules out the wire defects listed under *What it found*, but a
  bug the two happen to share would still pass. OpenSSL 3.5 now covers 1.2 plain PSK (it has no DTLS 1.3). The next
  one is Mbed TLS 3.6 (DTLS 1.2, RFC 9146 connection ID — the 1.2 CID's missing live peer, since Debian's wolfSSL
  5.9.1 fails it): its `ssl_server2` / `ssl_client2` from the sha256-pinned release tarball, built outside `modules/`
  (dual Apache-2.0 / GPL), driven as black boxes from `tools/interop.zig`. Not built yet: fetching and building it
  needs the owner's approval in this environment.
